must_remember: Both p-type and n-type regions of a Zener diode are heavily doped, leading to a narrow depletion region of the order of $10^{-6} \text{ m}$.
Zener breakdown occurs at low reverse voltages ($V_Z < 5\text{ V}$) due to high electric field ($> 10^6 \text{ V/m}$) direct rupture of covalent bonds.
Avalanche breakdown occurs at higher reverse voltages ($V_Z > 6\text{ V}$) due to impact ionization and cascading multiplication of charge carriers.
The dynamic resistance $r_z$ of a Zener diode in the breakdown region is extremely small, maintaining a constant voltage drop.
The temperature coefficient of Zener voltage is negative for $V_Z < 5\text{ V}$ (Zener dominant) and positive for $V_Z > 6\text{ V}$ (Avalanche dominant).

glossary.meaning: Quantum mechanical tunneling or direct field ionization of valence electrons across a narrow depletion region under a high electric field.
Carrier multiplication caused by impact ionization where high-energy minority carriers collide with lattice ions in wider depletion layers.
The small-signal resistance of the Zener diode in its breakdown region, defined as $r_z = \frac{\Delta V_Z}{\Delta I_Z}$.
A series resistor used in a Zener voltage regulator circuit to absorb excess input voltage fluctuations and limit the Zener current.
The capability of a regulator to maintain a nearly constant output voltage despite variations in load current.
